citeinfo.title: Toxicity of 6PPD alternatives to salmonid cell lines
citeinfo.othercit: Greer, J.B., E.M. Dalsky, P. Bachand, and J.D. Hansen. 2026. Toxicity of 6PPD alternatives to salmonid cell lines. WA Department of Ecology. IAA No. C2400057. https://www.ezview.wa.gov/Portals/_1962/Documents/6ppd/6PPD%20Alternatives%20Technical%20Memo.pdf

descript.abstract: Pollutants present in stormwater runoff can severely degrade water quality in aquatic habitats. The tire-derived chemical 6PPD-quinone is one such pollutant present in stormwater that is known to significantly impact the survival of salmonids. 6PPD-quinone is derived from 6PPD, the primary antiozonant used to protect tire rubber from ozone attack and degradation. Alternative antiozonants to replace 6PPD are currently being considered for automobile tires. In addition to acceptable tire performance the feasibility of any such replacement depends on minimizing environmental impacts. This data examines the toxicity of proposed alternative antiozonants using in vivo exposures and in vitro cell lines derived from coho salmon, Chinook salmon, and rainbow trout. Ozonated product mixtures and purified quinone transformation products derived from select antiozonants was also performed.
descript.purpose: These data were collected to provide cell line and in vivo assessments for the toxicity of 6PPD replacement chemicals and their ozonated transformation products in several salmonids. The data should be used as an initial data to assess tire rubber antiozonants for their toxicity to salmonids.

procstep.procdesc:
Gas-phase ozonation was performed on two PPDs (7PPD, IPPD) to generate transformation product mixtures. 6PPD was ozonated as a positive control to provide a basis for comparing the toxicity of 7PPD and IPPD to their ozonated mixtures. Before ozonation, parent compounds were dissolved in methanol and applied to 8” x 8” glass plates using a gas-tight syringe at 100 μg PPD/cm2. After the chemicals were applied, the plates were allowed to dry under a fume hood until the methanol was evaporated. Once dry, the plates were placed in a glass chamber receiving 0.5 L/min of positive pressure compressed air containing 50 ppmv ozone. Ozone concentrations entering and exiting the glass chamber were continuously monitored using a UV/Vis spectrophotometer.
Ozonation was considered complete after ozone consumption by the PPD mass on the plates had effectively ceased. Following complete ozonation the plates were removed from the chamber and eluted using absolute ethanol. The eluent was transferred into pre-weighed amber glass bottles and purged with N2 before storage at -20 degrees Celsius.For each ozonation experiment, one control plate with the same mass of PPD applied was placed in a vacuum chamber with compressed air for the duration of the ozonation process and eluted at he end of the experiment. The control and ozonated eluents were analyzed using targeted mass spectrometry to quantify the masses of the unreacted parent compounds and quinone transformation product. The ozonation of IPPD was performed twice due to rapid reaction rates. During the first ozonation, ozone reaction ceased at 5 hours, but the plate was ozonated for 24 hours to align with the ozonation times of 6PPD and 7PPD. Higher purity IPPD (TCI, 97.2% purity) was used for the second ozonation. The reaction again ceased early (6 hours), and the experiment was stopped.

The alamarBlue cell viability kit (Invitrogen) was used to quantify cellular metabolism. Briefly, CSE-119, CHSE-214, and RTG-2 cells were seeded in 96-well plates at a density of 10,000 cells per well in 100 µL of media and allowed to adhere for 24 hours. Stock solutions for parental antiozonants and purified quinone transformation product were serial diluted to 2X the desired final concentrations and added in 100 µL increments to each well to create the nominal concentrations of 0.1 - 200 µg/L, with at a minimum of 8 concentrations tested per cell line. Each chemical was dissolved overnight in absolute ethanol immediately prior to exposure. Transformation product mixtures for 7PPD, IPPD, and 6PPD were applied up to a maximum concentration of 200 micrograms per liter of the parent PPD.
Cell media containing the same percentage of ethanol as the highest chemical concentration (0.0067%) served as a solvent control. Each plate contained 4 replicates per concentration per cell type. Following chemical addition, the alamarBlue cell viability reagent was added to each well at 10% of the well volume in a dark room per the manufacture’s protocol. Fluorescence was measured at an excitation of 550 nm and emission of 600 nm with a gain of 70 using the Tecan Magellan Pro Infinite M Plex plate reader at the 0-, 6-, and 24-hour timepoints (+-10 min). Plates were kept covered with foil in a 20℃ incubator between measurements. Relative metabolism compared to solvent controls was calculated using measured fluorescence at 24 h compared to solvent controls from the same experiment at 6 h post-exposure.

The toxicity of the quinone transformation products of commercially available PPD alternatives was assessed in juvenile coho salmon (O. kisutch) (mass: 0.86 +- 0.02 g (mean +- standard error of mean)) obtained from the Issaquah salmon hatchery (Issaquah, WA). Fish were exposed in 8L of water inside of a 9L glass aquaria and supplied with constant aeration via air stone. Tanks were set on a water table with flowing water surrounding the tanks to ensure a constant temperature of 8 degrees Celsius (+- 0.5C). Fish were placed in 6L of water in the aquaria and allowed to acclimate for at least 1 h prior to the start of exposure. To ensure rapid mixing during exposure, 1L of fresh water was vigorously poured into each tank while 1 L of the appropriate chemical stock solution was added. Mortalities were then monitored for 24 h. No mortality was observed in any control treatments. A total of 8 fish were included in each replicate tank, with three replicate tanks per treatment.
